title: 45-day deadline to return a security deposit
summary: Within 45 days after a tenancy ends, the housing provider must either return the tenant's security deposit in full (with any interest owed) or give the tenant written notice of an intent to withhold all or part of it. If notice of withholding is given, the housing provider then has 30 days from that notice to deliver an itemized statement of the amounts withheld and to refund the balance.
tenant_action: Count 45 days from the last day of your tenancy. If neither the money nor a written withholding notice arrived, the deadline has passed and you can demand the full deposit in writing.

title: Itemized statement required for any amount withheld
summary: A housing provider who withholds part of a security deposit must provide a written, itemized statement of the specific deductions within 30 days of the withholding notice, and refund whatever is left over. A vague or unexplained deduction does not satisfy this requirement, and ordinary wear and tear is not a chargeable deduction.
tenant_action: If you received a lump-sum deduction with no itemization, ask in writing for the itemized statement the statute requires, and state that undocumented deductions are disputed.

title: Treble damages for bad-faith retention of a deposit
summary: If a housing provider retains a security deposit in bad faith — for example, by ignoring the statutory deadlines or inventing deductions — the tenant may recover up to three times the amount wrongfully withheld.
tenant_action: Naming the treble-damages exposure in your demand letter is often what moves a stalled deposit. Keep every dated piece of correspondence as evidence of bad faith.

title: Interest on deposits held 12 months or longer
summary: Security deposits must be held in an interest-bearing escrow account at a financial institution in the District. When a tenancy has lasted at least 12 months, the tenant is entitled to the interest that accrued on the deposit, paid out at the statutory rate when the deposit is returned.
tenant_action: If you lived there a year or more, your demand should ask for the deposit plus accrued interest, not just the principal.

title: Security deposit may not exceed one month's rent
summary: A housing provider in the District may not collect a security deposit greater than one month's rent, and the deposit must be held separately from the housing provider's own funds.
tenant_action: If you were charged more than one month's rent as a deposit, say so explicitly — the excess is recoverable.

title: Duty to keep the unit in habitable condition
summary: The District's Housing Code requires a housing provider to keep every rented unit and its common areas in a clean, safe, and sanitary condition — including structural soundness, working plumbing and heat, adequate light and ventilation, and control of insects and rodents. This duty applies from the first day of the tenancy and cannot be waived by the lease.
tenant_action: Put every repair request in writing with dates and photos. A written record is what turns a maintenance complaint into an enforceable housing-code claim.

title: Implied warranty of habitability in every DC lease
authority: Javins v. First National Realty Corp., 428 F.2d 1071 (D.C. Cir. 1970)
summary: Every residential lease in the District carries an implied warranty that the unit meets the Housing Code. Serious code violations are a breach of that warranty, and a tenant's obligation to pay full rent is tied to the housing provider's obligation to maintain the unit. Rent withholding is a recognized remedy, but it is risky: a tenant who withholds should be ready to pay the disputed rent into the court registry.
tenant_action: Do not simply stop paying rent. Document the conditions, notify the housing provider in writing, and get advice from OTA or a tenant attorney before withholding anything.
source_name: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

title: Requesting a housing-code inspection
summary: A tenant can request a free housing-code inspection of their unit through DC 311 or the Department of Buildings. An inspector's written report of violations is independent, third-party evidence that a housing provider's own records cannot contradict, and it is frequently the single most useful document in a repair dispute.
tenant_action: File a 311 request for a housing inspection and keep the service-request number. Requesting an inspection is protected activity — retaliating against you for it is illegal.

title: Retaliation is illegal, and is presumed within 6 months
summary: A housing provider may not take adverse action against a tenant — eviction, rent increase, reduction of services, or harassment — in retaliation for the tenant exercising a legal right, such as complaining to a government agency, requesting repairs, or organizing with other tenants. If the adverse action occurs within six months of the protected activity, the law presumes retaliation, and the housing provider must rebut that presumption by clear and convincing evidence.
tenant_action: Write down the date of your protected activity and the date of the adverse action. If they are within six months of each other, say so directly — the burden shifts to the housing provider.

title: Eviction requires a court order
summary: A tenant in the District may be evicted only for one of the causes listed in the Rental Housing Act, and only through a court proceeding that ends in a judgment for possession. The housing provider must first serve a written notice that states the specific cause and, where the violation can be cured, gives the tenant the opportunity to cure it before any case is filed.
tenant_action: A notice from your housing provider is not an eviction. Nothing can force you out until a court has ruled and a court-supervised eviction is scheduled. Never move out on the strength of a letter alone.

title: Self-help eviction (lockouts, utility shutoffs) is unlawful
summary: The District abolished self-help eviction: a housing provider may not change the locks, remove a tenant's belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out, even if the tenant is behind on rent. A tenant subjected to a self-help eviction has a claim for damages.
tenant_action: If you have been locked out or had utilities cut off, this is an emergency — call the police to report an illegal lockout and contact OTA the same day.

title: Limits on rent increases for rent-controlled units
summary: For units covered by rent stabilization, rent may generally be increased no more than once in any twelve-month period, and the increase is capped by a formula tied to the CPI-W published each year by the Rental Housing Commission. Lower caps apply to households headed by an elderly tenant or a tenant with a disability. Increases that exceed the applicable cap, or that come sooner than twelve months after the last one, are unlawful.
tenant_action: Check the date of your last increase and the current published cap before anything else — the twelve-month rule alone invalidates a surprising number of increases.

title: Written notice required before a rent increase
summary: A rent increase does not take effect unless the tenant has been given proper advance written notice, served in the manner the Rental Housing Act requires. A verbal announcement, a text message, or a notice that gives less than the required lead time does not make the new rent enforceable.
tenant_action: Keep the notice you received, including the envelope or message metadata showing when it arrived — the date of service is often the decisive fact.

title: Rent increases require a properly registered unit
summary: Every rental unit in the District must be registered with the Rental Accommodations Division, either as covered by rent stabilization or under a claimed exemption. A housing provider who has not properly registered the unit — or who claims an exemption they are not entitled to — generally may not lawfully impose a rent increase.
tenant_action: Ask the Rental Accommodations Division for your building's registration and exemption filings. An unregistered unit is a strong defense against an increase.
source_name: DC Department of Housing and Community Development

title: Damages available for Rental Housing Act violations
summary: A tenant who prevails on a Rental Housing Act claim may recover the amount by which the rent charged exceeded the lawful rent, and a knowing violation exposes the housing provider to treble damages plus a civil fine. Relief is sought by filing a tenant petition with the Rental Accommodations Division.
tenant_action: Rent overcharges compound month after month. The sooner you file, the larger the recoverable period and the smaller the amount you have already lost.

title: Lease clauses waiving tenant rights are unenforceable
summary: A provision in a lease that purports to waive a tenant's rights under the District's housing laws is generally void and unenforceable. The fact that a tenant signed a lease containing such a clause does not give it effect.
tenant_action: If your housing provider is pointing at a lease clause, check whether the clause waives a statutory right — if it does, it does not bind you.

title: Three-year limitations period for most tenant claims
summary: Most contract and property claims in the District, including a claim for a wrongfully withheld security deposit, must be brought within three years of when the claim arose.
tenant_action: If your dispute is more than a couple of years old, treat filing as urgent rather than optional.

title: Small Claims Court for money disputes up to $10,000
authority: D.C. Superior Court, Small Claims and Conciliation Branch
summary: The Small Claims and Conciliation Branch of D.C. Superior Court hears money claims up to $10,000. Tenants may file without a lawyer, the filing fee is modest, and security-deposit cases are among the most common filings.
tenant_action: Bring your lease, your written demand, proof of delivery, and a simple dated timeline. Cases are usually won on documentation rather than argument.

title: Office of the Tenant Advocate (free help for DC tenants)
authority: D.C. Office of the Tenant Advocate
summary: The D.C. Office of the Tenant Advocate provides free advice, education, and in some cases legal representation to District tenants, and can direct a tenant to the right filing venue. Reach OTA at (202) 719-6560 or ota.dc.gov.
tenant_action: Call OTA before a deadline passes, not after. Advice is free and their intake staff will tell you which agency actually handles your issue.
source_name: D.C. Office of the Tenant Advocate
